chapters.label: Prologue
chapters.title: The Watch
chapters.html:
I am sitting here with an antique pocket watch in my hand. It was my grandfather’s.

He died in 1961, five years before I was born, and the watch stayed with my grandmother, whom everyone called Nan. One day she set it in my hand. She told me it had belonged to him and that he had brought it over from Scotland. Inside the case, engraved in the metal, was a single word. Edinburgh.

When I was a little boy, Nan and I would talk, and our talk always found its way back to Laurence. She would tell me how much I reminded her of him and that I was named after him. She could give me something of the man she had known. The years before she knew him were harder to get at.

Two days after he died, the Pawtucket Times carried his obituary. It named the father and mother who raised him, his wife and daughters, and a sister in Chicago. The newspaper gave Edinburgh as his birthplace. It was the same city Nan had shown me inside the watch. I could have taken those particulars to a Scottish registrar and asked for the birth of a Douglas boy, son of Robert and Elizabeth, in June 1907. I would have walked away without him.

On the page where his birth appears, he has another surname. His mother was Agnes Brown, born at Edston in Peeblesshire. I have followed the names through censuses and school registers, from the manifests of Atlantic ships to a courtroom in Pennsylvania. At the far end of the journey is a man my mother remembers as her father. At the beginning is a baby his mother called Lawrence Brown.

Sources and record notes
  1. Pawtucket Times, March 11, 1961, p. 3. Newspaper account of birth, parents and survivors.
  2. St Giles statutory births, 1907, entry 839. The watch and the childhood conversations come from the author.

chapters.label: Chapter 1
chapters.title: The Plowmen
chapters.html:
On census night in 1911 he was three years old, and he was recorded as the son of the house. He lived with Lizzie Douglas and her daughter Janet in Tollcross, Edinburgh. Robert Douglas was the man his school would name as guardian. Half a century later, when he died in Rhode Island, his obituary named Robert and Lizzie as his father and mother.

Behind the name my mother knew was another family. To find them I had to go back to Peeblesshire and to the generation of farm workers whose children carried McGarth and Tweedie in their names.

In 1851 the census index finds a McGarth family in Tweedsmuir. The father was Tweedie McGarth. His wife Jane came from Wamphray, across the county line in Dumfriesshire. Their household included Jane, Agnes, James Tweedie, Sarah, Ann and Janet. In a district where the same Christian names recur in family after family, that small cluster of names helped me recognize them across generations.

Tweedie and Jane’s daughter Agnes married William Brown, a plowman. Their son George’s death entry is unusually valuable to our family. It gives William’s trade and his wife’s maiden name. The person supplying the particulars was William himself. Years after the births of his children, a working man’s signature in the death register still tells us exactly where McGarth belongs in the family.

Two sons of William and Agnes figure in my grandfather’s story. An index to the Peebles birth records gives September 14, 1860, for Lawrence Tweedie Brown. It names both his parents. In 1871 the census places Lawrence, ten, and his younger brother George, eight, in the same household. George also became a plowman. At twenty he married Christina Henderson of Quothquan, across the hills in the upper valley of the Clyde.

The names traveled in more than one direction. Lawrence’s middle name had belonged to the McGarth side. When George and Christina had their second daughter, they called her Agnes McGarth Brown, giving the baby her paternal grandmother’s married name in full. In our family the understanding is that this Agnes named her son for her father’s older brother. Agnes registered her child as Lawrence Brown. The register tells us how she spelled his name. The reason she chose it comes from the family.

Lawrence Tweedie Brown married Isabella Graham. The family’s research follows the couple through Scottish censuses and into Quebec, where a burial record for a son names both parents. It was the younger brother, George, whose daughter would one day bring the name Lawrence back onto a Scottish birth register.

William Brown lived to report the death of the younger of those two boys. When George died in 1886, his daughter Agnes was still an infant. A generation later, part of what she could give a child of her own was a name that had belonged in her father’s house before she was born.

Sources and record notes
  1. Peebles deaths, 1886, entry 14. Names George’s parents and William Brown as informant.
  2. Lawrence Tweedie Brown, birth index, Peebles, September 14, 1860. The family’s notes identify the 1851 Tweedsmuir census as an index transcription.
  3. 1871 Scotland census index, the brothers in William Brown’s household. The Quebec burial reference and identification of Isabella Graham are in the family’s research notes. Naming for the uncle is family testimony.
  4. Peebles, entry 149, 1885. George reports his daughter Agnes McGarth Brown.

chapters.label: Chapter 2
chapters.title: Agnes
chapters.html:
Agnes Brown was born a week before Christmas. Before she was four months old her father was dead. We have the birth entries for two sisters and a death entry for their father from which to piece together those first years of her family. One birth entry was supplied by her mother, another by her father, and in the death register the informant was her grandfather.

Her parents married on Friday, June 1, 1883, at Quothquan in the parish of Libberton. George Brown was a plowman. Christina Henderson was a daughter of Alexander Henderson and Jane Robb. The place and date of their marriage were carried into the records of both their daughters. At a time when a family could move to another farm in another parish and leave little paper behind, those repeated particulars help identify them on either side of a county line.

Their first girl was born on August 18, 1883, at twenty past eight in the morning in Quothquan. They called her Mary Henderson Brown. Christina reported the birth on September 5. Henderson, the surname Christina had given up at marriage, went into her little girl’s name. Two years later a name from George’s side went into her sister’s.

At half past two on Friday afternoon, December 18, 1885, the second girl was born at Edston. George reported her birth at Peebles on the last day of that year. The handwritten entry is Agnes McGarth Brown. The modern heading attached to the image spells the middle name McGrath. There is a real difference in where the letters fall. It is there on a single copy of one record, a reminder of how easily a family can go missing in an index.

George Brown died at Edston at half past one on the morning of Monday, April 5, 1886. He was twenty-three. The doctor who certified the causes was Alexander Ferguson. He gave pleuro-pneumonia of twenty-one days and asthenia, a term for weakness. The people who wrote the register could put a duration to his illness and an hour to his death. The man who brought them those particulars was William Brown, George’s father.

Mary was two years old. Agnes was a little over three months. On the last day of December George had signed as father to a daughter. Barely more than three months later William signed as father to the son he had lost. I know of no letter from the young widow about what she did next. The next place I can put Christina’s girls together is in her own parish, with the Henderson women.

Sources and record notes
  1. Peebles births, 768/00 0149, registered December 31, 1885. Compare the handwritten name with the image heading.
  2. Peebles deaths, 768/00 0014, certified causes, duration and informant. Mary Henderson Brown’s 1883 birth is Libberton 650/00 0015, p. 5, as cited in the family’s register notes.

chapters.label: Chapter 3
chapters.title: The Cottages at Quothquan
chapters.html:
The census of 1891 takes up the girls' story in their mother's village of Quothquan, in the upper valley of the Clyde. By then Agnes Brown was five, and she had already lost her father.

The census called the row Castle. A crofter, a mole catcher, a dressmaker, a stonebreaker and a farm servant were among the people recorded there. Janet Paterson, seventy-eight, was listed in a household of her own. The people on either side of her in the enumeration included members of two families that recur throughout Agnes’s childhood.

Christina had died at Quothquan that February. Her name is on the Henderson family monument. Her two girls had now lost both parents.

When the census was taken on the night of Sunday, April 5, both girls were living with Christina's mother. The census listed their grandmother, Jane Henderson, as fifty-six, born at Carnwath, and head of the household. Her daughter Jane, twenty-seven, was the dressmaker. Her youngest son, Andrew, was still at school. Mary Brown was seven. Agnes Brown was five. The return calls them Jane's granddaughters.

Another young man lived with them. James Parker, eighteen and born at Biggar, was working as an agricultural laborer. Ten years earlier, when James was eight, the census had called him an adopted son and listed him as a scholar. In 1891 he was entered simply as adopted. Even on a census page, the differences in how the children had come into the house were visible. Ten years later another census would find Agnes and James under the same roof.

A few entries away lived Ann Archibald, a widow. Her husband, George, had died in April 1885. Her daughter was Mary Archibald. One son, Alexander, was a stonebreaker. The other, John, was working on a farm. Only one household stood between the Archibalds and the Hendersons in the enumerator's book. Ten years later members of both families were still in the village, though in different households, and their names would keep turning up beside one another in this story.

That spring and summer the two households lost people within days of one another. Jane Henderson died on June 8, four months after her daughter Christina. John Archibald died on June 20, four days after his eighteenth birthday. The dates survive in the monumental inscriptions in Quothquan churchyard.

By midsummer Agnes had lost her father, her mother and the grandmother in whose house the census had found her that April. She was five and a half years old. Among the people whose names I can still trace are her sister Mary, her aunt Jane, her young uncle Andrew, and James Parker, the boy who had been taken into the same house years before her.

Sources and record notes
  1. Libberton census, Castle, schedules 5–7, index. Degrees of relationship, occupations and ages.
  2. Mary and the Archibald household, 1891 census index. The Henderson and Archibald monumental inscriptions are cited in the family’s churchyard notes. The two transcriptions for Christina differ on the day in February.
  3. 1881 census index for James Parker, Libberton, ED 3, p. 4, household 18.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: The Knight of Shieldhill
chapters.html:
In the summer of 1907 one place name appeared in two very different records. Agnes gave Shieldhill, Biggar, as part of her address when she registered her son. Later that month it appeared in the London Gazette beside the name of a new knight.

Nathaniel Dunlop had been born at Campbeltown, on the Kintyre peninsula. In 1847 he entered the Glasgow counting house of George Gillespie, whose business handled work for the Allan shipping line. In 1853 Dunlop joined the Allan firm itself. The Allan Line's steamers carried Scottish emigrants across the Atlantic to Quebec and Montreal. He came to run the shipping business and to chair the Clyde Navigation Trust, which oversaw navigation on the river where so many ships were built.

The estate at Shieldhill, long held by the Chancellor family, came into his possession in 1898. The mansion incorporated an old stone tower. Its farms and cottages extended the estate far beyond the house itself, down to the village of Quothquan.

Dunlop’s knighthood took effect on June 28, 1907, a fortnight after Agnes Brown gave birth. On July 4 she gave Shieldhill as part of her home address to the registrar in Edinburgh. Between the date attached to the honor and the day of the investiture, her son had acquired an entry in the public records of his own.

On Monday, July 15, Edward VII conferred the knighthood at Buckingham Palace. The Gazette preserves a list rather than a scene. On it with Dunlop are the painter Hubert von Herkomer, James Donaldson of the University of St Andrews, and William Schwenck Gilbert, whose words audiences knew from The Mikado and H.M.S. Pinafore. The address printed after Dunlop’s name was Shieldhill, Biggar.

The Gazette published the list on July 26. Like the entry for my grandfather’s birth, it can be read by anyone who knows where to look. On the honours list the place name followed the landowner. On the birth entry it followed a young woman who worked for a living.

From then on, in the parish, he was Sir Nathaniel. The honor belonged to him. The address belonged to a place where a great many people made their living, on its farms, in its gardens and in its cottages. To follow Agnes, we have to leave the list of honours and look at the houses below his.

Sources and record notes
  1. The London Gazette, July 26, 1907, p. 5118, list of the July 15 investiture and effective date.
  2. Contemporary knightage entry, Nathaniel Dunlop of Shieldhill.
  3. Modern Shipbuilding and the Men Engaged in It, career sketch of Nathaniel Dunlop, counting house and Allan firm.
  4. The use of Shieldhill in the manuscript comes from Agnes’s own entry.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Shieldhill
chapters.html:
Shieldhill sits on the north side of the upper Clyde. Behind the village rises the green dome of Quothquan Law. Across the valley to the southwest stands Tinto, the highest hill in the district. Between them lie farmland, stone dykes, the river in its meadows and the woods of the estate. At the top of the road stood Shieldhill House, a mansion built up around an old stone tower, with parts dating back to the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

By March 1901, the enumerator at Quothquan had names for the cottages. At Gean Tree lived Mary Archibald, listed as thirty-five, a sewing mistress. Another household at Gean Tree consisted of James Grossart, an eighty-year-old road surfaceman, and his granddaughter Marion. At Lime Tree Cottage the head of the house was Andrew Henderson.

Andrew was twenty-five and a groom. Local people later remembered "Andrew Henderson, late of Lime Tree," as a poet who wrote about the district and a keeper of bees. His nieces were still together. Mary Brown was seventeen and Agnes was fifteen. James Parker, who had lived with their grandmother, appears again, this time as a boarder. He was twenty-eight and had become a gamekeeper.

The names tell us something about the village that an estate address alone cannot. Gean is a Scots name for the wild cherry. Lime Tree and Gean Tree were distinct addresses. A later history of the parish says Lime Tree Cottage became part of the house known as Geantree. The row once called Castle is known today as Huntfield Place. The census gives the order in which the houses were recorded. It would take more than the numbers on that page to say who shared a wall.

For generations the Chancellor family had owned Shieldhill. The village account places the sale to Nathaniel Dunlop of the Allan Line in 1898 and describes the rebuilding of houses in the row. His daughter, Ellen Smith Dunlop, also has a place in the parish’s history.

The parish church stood at Libberton. The old church at Quothquan was a ruin. In 1903 Nathaniel and Ellen Dunlop built Shieldhill Hall for evening worship. Historic Environment Scotland’s listing identifies its builders and the use for which it was intended.

The Dunlop name turns up again at Thankerton. Local histories credit Ellen Smith Dunlop with helping to establish the creamery there in 1911. The parish also records the inauguration of its Women’s Rural Institute at Shieldhill Hall in 1918. Those landmarks give the estate a history outside its big house.

The big house needed people: servants for the house, gardeners for the grounds, keepers for the woods. Mary Archibald's brother Alexander was now a domestic gardener. The census gave his address, and his wife Annie's, as Shieldhill. In August 1903 James Parker married Janet Crawford Stewart. He signed himself James Lawson Parker and gave his occupation and address as gamekeeper at Shieldhill, Biggar. By 1911 the Parkers had a home at Shieldhill Mains, with three children, John, Euphemia and Robert.

Agnes appears in the records as a domestic servant. Her employer's name has yet to turn up. The address she gave was Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar.

Sources and record notes
  1. Historic Environment Scotland, Shieldhill House, LB7377. The family’s parish research identifies the village account of the estate sale and the cottage rebuilds as a later local history.
  2. 1901 Libberton census index, the households at Lime Tree and Gean Tree.
  3. 1901 census index for Alexander Archibald, domestic gardener at Shieldhill.
  4. James Lawson Parker and Janet Crawford Stewart, 1903 marriage entry. The 1911 Libberton return names their children.
  5. Libberton and Quothquan parish history, evening worship and the Women’s Rural Institute. The creamery and Andrew Henderson’s poetry and beekeeping are attributed to local histories in the family’s research.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: Lizzie
chapters.html:
While Agnes was growing up in Lanarkshire, the woman who would raise her son was living a different life on the south side of Edinburgh. Her name was Elizabeth Miller McDonald. In the family she was Lizzie.

Lizzie was born on May 31, 1874, at Gilmerton, in the parish of Liberton, near Edinburgh. This Liberton, spelled with one b, was a different parish from the Libberton near Biggar where Agnes Brown grew up. The resemblance of those names can make two families look nearer to one another on paper than they were.

Lizzie’s mother, Ann McDonald, married Robert Hope. The Hope family account takes them to New Zealand aboard the Rakaia in 1878. While the ship was at sea Ann had a son. The name John Rakaia Hope in the New Zealand birth index preserves the name of the ship. Lizzie was four that year. The next Scottish census found her growing up with her grandparents.

In 1881 Lizzie was six and living on the Main Road at Gilmerton with her grandparents, John McDonald and Janet Page. Both were fifty-two. Three of their own children were still at home: George, twenty-five, Janet, fifteen, and Alexander, twelve. The census calls Lizzie their grandchild and gives her occupation as scholar.

Ten years later Lizzie was sixteen and working as a live-in domestic servant at 14 Wilson Road in Liberton. There were four young boys in the household and another servant, Catherine Davidson.

On June 9, 1899, at 34 St Patrick Square in Edinburgh, Lizzie married Robert Douglas. The minister was W. Whyte Smith of Newington Free Church, and the wedding followed the forms of the Free Church of Scotland. The witnesses were James Finlayson and Janet Page Moodie. Lizzie was a domestic servant, living at 4 Hatton Place. Robert was twenty-three, a sawmiller, living at 29 St Leonards Terrace. He had been born on May 8, 1876, at 9 Canon Street, Edinburgh, the son of Archibald Douglas, then a wood merchant's traveller and later a forester, and Isabella Gray.

The marriage entry gave Lizzie's age as twenty-four, although her twenty-fifth birthday had passed nine days earlier. In the places set aside for her parents are the names John McDonald, coal salesman, and Janet McDonald, born Page. They were the grandparents in whose house the census had found her as a girl.

Family records give their daughter Janet Page Douglas a birthday of April 29, 1900. Janet and Page were the given name and maiden surname of the grandmother who had raised Lizzie. In the spring of 1901 the census found the family at 5 Beaumont Place in Edinburgh. Robert was working as a stone machineman. Lizzie was twenty-six. Janet was eleven months old.

Our family also remembers a daughter called Isabella Gray Douglas who died in infancy. Her name was the name of Robert's mother. I have yet to find her birth or death entry. In 1911 the census listed ten-year-old Janet in Lizzie's household as daughter and three-year-old Laurence as son. Why she and Robert took him in was never written down in any record I have seen.

Sources and record notes
  1. Liberton statutory births, 693/70, p. 24. Ann McDonald, domestic servant, identified herself as mother.
  2. 1881 census, Gilmerton, schedule 141. Elizabeth is entered as grandchild.
  3. 1891 census, 14 Wilson Road, Liberton.
  4. Edinburgh statutory marriages 685/4 213. Names, witnesses and stated parental relationships.
  5. Robert’s statutory birth, St George district, 1876, 685/1 845.
  6. 1901 census at Beaumont Place. The Hope family account and NZ birth index distinguish John Rakaia Hope. Isabella Gray Douglas is identified here as family recollection.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The Autumn of 1906
chapters.html:
In the autumn of 1906 Agnes Brown was twenty. Her twenty-first birthday would fall a week before Christmas. It is the season our family has gone back to more often than any other in her life. A child born the following June might have been conceived that autumn, assuming a pregnancy that went to term. His birth entry gives the time of the delivery to the hour. It gives no measure of the weeks that came before it.

In the last census taken before that autumn, Agnes was fifteen and Mary seventeen. The two sisters were living with their uncle Andrew Henderson at Lime Tree Cottage. James Parker, an agricultural laborer when he and the girls lived with their grandmother, had become a gamekeeper. Their uncle was a groom. In a family whose work was bound up with land and the people who owned it, the men’s occupations are relatively easy to follow. Five years passed between that census and the autumn of 1906. There is no surviving wage book among the family papers to tell us when she took her first place.

Women in the family and in the neighboring cottages earned their own livings. Her aunt Jane had earned her living as a dressmaker. Mary Archibald, a crofter’s daughter in the village where the Brown girls grew up, was listed as a sewing mistress in 1901. Her brother Alexander had become a gardener at Shieldhill. Mary’s address in that census was Gean Tree. When Agnes next gave an address of her own, one word in the name of the cottage would lead us back to this little group of households.

The village had acquired a new place to meet. In 1903 Nathaniel Dunlop and Miss E. Dunlop had a hall built at Quothquan for evening worship. The parish history remembers services at six on Sundays, with the Reverend John Picken and the Reverend Dr. Inglis Wardrope of Biggar taking turns. A great deal about a small place can survive in that fashion. I can find the name of a parish minister, the purpose of a building and even the hour at which its doors were open on a Sunday. Who went in with whom on any particular evening is another matter.

Where Agnes herself appears again, she is earning a living in domestic service and giving Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar, as her home. Her employer’s name is missing. So is the name my family most wanted to find, the father of the child she was carrying. Nothing in the entries for the estate or the neighboring cottages gives me grounds to fill the space Agnes left on her son’s birth record. What those entries do give us back is the company in which she grew up. Her sister, her aunt, the uncle who took the girls in and the neighbors whose working lives ran alongside theirs all had names. They deserve to keep their places in her story.

Sources and record notes
  1. Libberton census, 1891 and 1901. The family archive has index transcriptions for the cottage households. Occupations for Mary Archibald, James Parker and Andrew Henderson are also recorded in the research notes to Chapters 5 and 11.
  2. Historic Environment Scotland, Shieldhill Hall, LB12995. The parish history records the six o’clock services and names the ministers.
  3. The 1907 birth entry identifies Agnes’s domicile and occupation. Its date supports the conditional timing of a pregnancy. Its parent column identifies only Agnes.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 8
chapters.title: The Road to Edinburgh
chapters.html:
On the same line of an Edinburgh birth register, two places that belonged to Agnes Brown appear a long way apart. Under the heading for her child’s birthplace is the Royal Maternity Hospital, Edinburgh. Beside Agnes’s name and occupation is her own domicile, Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar. One was where my grandfather was born. The other was the place his mother still called home when she registered his birth in July.

The postal name Biggar can send a reader to the town itself. The census records that put Agnes with her uncle lead into the countryside of Libberton parish near Quothquan. In the 1901 enumeration, the schedules for Gean Tree Cottages and Lime Tree Cottage follow one another. Mary Archibald appears at one, the Hendersons and the Brown girls at the other. Six years later, the name Agnes supplied was specific enough to include a cottage and an estate as well as a post town. She had a rural address of her own to give in the capital.

One way out of that part of Clydesdale was by rail. Across the Clyde at Thankerton there had been a station since 1848. The Caledonian Railway connected the district through Carstairs with Edinburgh. On a map the line passes names familiar from the family records. One is Carnwath, the birthplace given for Agnes’s grandmother. Nearer the city come Midcalder and Slateford. The Caledonian terminus was Princes Street Station at the west end of Edinburgh. There was a real, established connection between the two places on the birth record. I have no ticket, letter or witness who can put Agnes on a particular train.

Edinburgh had more than one place where a woman could go to give birth. In 1904 Dr. Elsie Inglis had opened a hospital for women and children at 219 High Street, known as the Hospice and staffed by women. The institution named on my grandfather’s record had a different history. Its purpose-built maternity hospital had stood on Lauriston Place since 1879. In 1895 it added a pavilion for married women. The identification matters because the institutions kept their own records. To look for Agnes’s admission, ours is the hospital at number 79.

The university archive that holds the maternity hospital’s papers lists indoor casebooks and birth registers covering 1907. A hospital entry might give the date Agnes arrived or tell us how long she stayed. I have yet to find Agnes by name in either series. For now I can follow her from the address she gave to the place of the delivery. The date she left the cottage belongs to the part of the journey we still hope to recover. The date and hour at the other end are in her son’s record.

Sources and record notes
  1. Libberton, 1901 census index, schedules 13–15, and St Giles birth entry 839, 1907. The two places occur under different headings.
  2. Railway and Canal Historical Society, Railway Passenger Stations in Great Britain. The line via Carstairs describes a possible connection. No record here identifies Agnes’s journey.
  3. Historic Environment Scotland, 79 Lauriston Place, LB44033, including the 1895 pavilion.
  4. Curious Edinburgh, site of the Hospice, opened at 219 High Street in 1904.
  5. Lothian Health Services Archive, Edinburgh Royal Maternity Hospital fonds LHB3. Family research identifies indoor casebook LHB3/14/6 and birth register LHB3/16/3 as volumes to consult for 1907. An entry for Agnes has yet to be established.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 9
chapters.title: Born at Nine O’Clock
chapters.html:
At nine o’clock on Friday evening, June 14, 1907, Agnes Brown gave birth to my grandfather at the Royal Maternity Hospital in Edinburgh. She was twenty-one. Inside the case of the watch my grandmother gave me is the word Edinburgh. For a long time that one word was about as close as I could get to the place where his life began. I can give my mother a street and an hour now, and I can tell her who supplied the information. Her father’s first record says “Agnes Brown, Mother.”

The hospital stood at 79 Lauriston Place. The building is still recognizable by its high arched entrance, with two wooden doors beneath a fanlight. In the wards, the upper sections of the tall windows could be opened separately. The building had opened on May 1, 1879, paid for by public subscription as a memorial to Sir James Young Simpson. Edinburgh people had raised money in a doctor’s name for a place where women could have their babies. Agnes was born six years after its doors opened.

There were two kinds of work going on there. Women came to Lauriston Place for their confinements, and the hospital also sent staff out to deliveries in Edinburgh homes. House surgeons, nurses, pupil midwives and medical students took part in the work. By the time Agnes arrived, one bed had been set aside for a purpose that had taken a physician years to establish. John William Ballantyne wanted women who needed treatment during pregnancy to be able to enter the hospital before they went into labor. The endowed bed opened in November 1901. Its history tells us something about the hospital Agnes entered. Our family’s papers have yet to yield the name of the person who attended her own delivery.

Three hours before Agnes’s son was born, an observer at Leith recorded fifty-nine degrees Fahrenheit, a light west wind and an overcast sky. At eight that morning it had been fifty-two, with cloud and no wind. By eight the next morning the station had measured four hundredths of an inch of rain over the preceding twenty-four hours. Those are observations from Leith. The hour at Lauriston Place comes from Agnes.

In the St Giles register her son is entry 839. His name is Lawrence Brown, spelled with a w. The space for his father is blank. Agnes gave her occupation as domestic servant and her home as Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar. The entry I have is in Edinburgh. Anyone looking only under Douglas, the surname my mother knew as her own, could pass right over him.

There is another mother on that page. Six days after my grandfather was born, Barbara Bisset Sherra gave birth to a daughter in the same hospital, at a quarter past seven in the evening. She named her Mary Caldwell Sherra. Barbara, too, was a domestic servant. Where Agnes had been able to give the name of a cottage, the words entered for Barbara were “none fixed.” On July 4 both women registered their babies. Their names appear one below the other. Each signed as the child’s mother.

When Agnes herself was born at Edston, it was her father, George Brown, who reported the birth. His entry gives the hour too, half past two in the afternoon on December 18, 1885. He died the following April. Agnes was five when she lost her mother, Christina Henderson. Neither lived to see the entry for their grandson. At twenty-one their daughter did for her child what her father had once done for her. Twenty days after the birth on Lauriston Place, she put his name on record.

Edinburgh birth register, entry 839

Name as entered, Lawrence Brown. Born June 14, 1907, at 9 p.m., Royal Maternity Hospital, Edinburgh. Mother and informant, Agnes Brown, domestic servant. Domicile, Gean Cottage, Shieldhill, Biggar. Registered July 4, 1907, St Giles.

Sources and record notes
  1. National Records of Scotland, St Giles statutory births, 1907, 685/04 0839, page 280. Rows 838–840 give Phyllis Campbell Flynn, Lawrence Brown and Mary Caldwell Sherra. The latter two births were registered July 4 by their mothers.
  2. Peebles statutory births, 1885, entry 149, and George Brown’s statutory death entry, 1886. The month of Christina Henderson’s death is supported by the family’s monumental-inscription research. The watch and its engraving are the author’s family evidence.
  3. Lothian Health Services Archive, Edinburgh Royal Maternity Hospital history, opening, funding, teaching and care in the district.
  4. Historic Environment Scotland, LB44033, doorway and ward windows.
  5. J. W. Ballantyne, British Medical Journal, February 5, 1916, p. 189. His account dates the Hamilton Bed to November 1901.
  6. Meteorological Office, Daily Weather Report, June 14–15, 1907, Leith observations. The rain figure covers the full observation interval ending at eight on June 15.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 10
chapters.title: His First Name
chapters.html:
The first man I went looking for in Scotland was Laurence Brown Douglas. If I had insisted on finding all three names together in the Edinburgh birth register, I would never have found my grandfather. His entry is under Brown. The first name is Lawrence, with a w. And the day to look for, if one is following the registrar page by page, is a Thursday in July, twenty days after he was born.

The Post Office directory for Edinburgh and Leith lists R. D. Robertson in two different parts of the book. In the alphabetical directory he is the registrar for St Giles. The office was at 24 Forrest Road and his own home was on Marchmont Road. Turn to the street directory and number 24 appears again, this time with the registrar’s office, Robertson’s name and the name of his assistant, James Lamond. It is Robertson’s signature that appears at the foot of my grandfather’s entry on July 4, 1907.

Scottish law gave twenty-one days to report a birth. The law also allowed a name to be added later if the child had been registered without one. That difference matters in our family because the twenty-day interval once made it sound as though Agnes had spent nearly three weeks trying to name her son. Nothing she signed tells us when she chose his name. It tells us that when the birth was registered, he had one. In our family it was understood that she named him for Lawrence Tweedie Brown, her father George’s older brother. The name appears in the family before the baby was born. The reason for choosing it has come down by word of mouth.

I went back to the entries immediately before and after his. Above him is Phyllis Campbell Flynn, born on June 17 in Drummond Street to Margaret Flynn, a laundress. Below him is Mary Caldwell Sherra, born on June 20 at the Royal Maternity Hospital to Barbara Bisset Sherra. Both girls were born after the boy between them. Phyllis’s birth was registered on July 3. His and Mary’s were registered on July 4. There is the reason my grandfather occupies that particular line on page 280. The children came into the register in the order their births were reported.

For Agnes, the form gave space to two kinds of information in the same entry. Under parentage it calls her a domestic servant and supplies her home address. Under informant it gives her name again and tells us in what capacity she supplied the particulars. Mother. No father’s name appears. Going on from that page through school records, passenger lists and American citizenship papers, I would find more than one spelling of the boy’s name and more than one account of who his parents were. This earliest one is hers. She called him Lawrence Brown.

Sources and record notes
  1. Post Office Edinburgh and Leith Directory, 1907–08, printed pp. 328 and 532. The alphabetical entry and the Forrest Road entry agree on the office.
  2. Registration of Births, Deaths and Marriages (Scotland) Act 1854, sections 27, 32 and 33. The deadline concerned reporting the birth. The date Agnes chose the name is unknown.
  3. National Records of Scotland, St Giles, statutory births, 1907, p. 280, entries 838–840. Naming the child for Lawrence Tweedie Brown is attributed to family testimony in the author’s Chapter 10 notes.

chapters.part: Part Two: The Year of the Child
chapters.label: Chapter 11
chapters.title: The Missing Years
chapters.html:
When my grandfather was twenty days old, his mother gave the Edinburgh registrar the name of a cottage near Biggar. When he was three years old, the census found him in the middle of Edinburgh with a family called Douglas. I can follow Agnes’s people through those years. I can even find out who was living at the cottages when the census taker came round again. The one person I went there looking for is the child who disappears between those two entries.

Agnes knew what it was to be taken in by family. After her mother died in February 1891, the census found her and her sister Mary living with their grandmother in Libberton parish. The address in the index is simply Castle. Jane Henderson, their grandmother, was fifty-six and earned her living as a crofter. Her daughter Jane was a dressmaker. Mary Brown, seven, and Agnes Brown, five, were entered as granddaughters. James Parker, eighteen, an agricultural laborer, lived in the household too. The family had taken him in years before. The census used the word “Adopted” for him.

Ten years later the two Brown girls still appear together, this time at Lime Tree Cottage. Their uncle Andrew Henderson was twenty-five. Mary was seventeen and Agnes fifteen. James Parker, now twenty-eight, was there again, entered this time as a boarder. In the same enumeration district, the neighboring schedules give the name Gean Tree Cottages. Mary Archibald appears under that address. Both cottage names belong to the surviving account of Agnes’s youth. In 1907, when the registrar asked for her domicile, the name he wrote was Gean Cottage.

In the spring of 1911 the rural census takes us back to that neighborhood in considerable detail. Andrew Rodger, a farmer of sixty-five, and his wife Jane, forty-six, occupied Gean Tree Cottage. The return counted three rooms with windows. At Shieldhill Mains, James Parker was still working as a gamekeeper. His wife Janet was thirty-four. Their children were John, five, Euphemia, three, and Robert, one. Euphemia was my grandfather’s age. The two children appear in the same census, one with the Parkers in the parish where Agnes had grown up, the other in Edinburgh.

James Parker had shared a home with Agnes. Gean Tree was a cottage name the family could trace. We have no account of what contact she had with the people living there in 1911. It would be easy to put the baby in one of them after she left the hospital. The first census after his birth came nearly four years later. It could tell us who was under a roof on the night of April 2, 1911. It could say nothing about a cradle that might have stood there in 1907 or 1908.

Scotland’s system of legal adoption came into operation in 1930. My grandfather was a grown man by then. There is no reason to expect a Scottish adoption order from his infancy to tell my mother the date her father went to the Douglases. The date I can give her is the first one on which I can place him there. On that Sunday night in 1911, a ten-year-old girl named Janet was entered on a census page in Edinburgh. On the line immediately beneath hers was her little brother.

Sources and record notes
  1. Libberton census, 1891, Castle, schedule 7. The copy available for this household is an index transcription.
  2. Libberton census, 1901, ED 3 p. 3, schedules 13–15. Lime Tree and Gean Tree are distinguished in the index.
  3. Libberton census, 1911, ED 3 p. 2. The original return gives the Parkers’ names and occupations and the Rodgers at Gean Tree Cottage.
  4. Edinburgh census, 1911, St Giles 685/4, ED 69 p. 11. The original page places Laurence at 16 Lochrin Place.
  5. National Records of Scotland, Adoption Records, guidance on private arrangements before 1930.

chapters.label: Chapter 12
chapters.title: The Douglases
chapters.html:
The address was 16 Lochrin Place, in Tollcross, within walking distance of the hospital where my grandfather was born. I had followed a cottage name out into Lanarkshire looking for the little boy. The first time I could find him with his new family, he was back in the city of his birth. On the census page for Sunday, April 2, 1911, Elizabeth Douglas appears at the top, followed by Janet, ten, and Laurence B., three.

Elizabeth was Lizzie to the family. She was born at Gilmerton on May 31, 1874, at two o’clock in the morning. The woman who reported her birth was Ann McDonald, a domestic servant. No father was named. Thirty-three years separate that entry and the one for Lawrence Brown. In each case the mother herself gave the registrar the particulars of her child. By the time the two children in those birth entries appear together, one is a woman of thirty-six and the other a boy who has yet to turn four.

Robert Douglas and Elizabeth Miller McDonald had married on June 9, 1899, at 34 St Patrick Square in Edinburgh, according to the forms of the Free Church of Scotland. Robert was twenty-three, a sawmiller living at 29 St Leonards Terrace. Lizzie was in domestic service and gave 4 Hatton Place as her home. Among the witnesses was a woman named Janet Page Moodie. Janet and Page were both names that carried into the next generation. The daughter who grew up beside Laurence was Janet Page Douglas.

In 1901 Janet was eleven months old. The census index places her with Robert and Lizzie at 5 Beaumont Place. Ten years later she was a schoolgirl at Lochrin Place. The boy beside her was Edinburgh-born, as she was. His given names are entered as “Laurence B.” Agnes had registered him as Lawrence, with a w. This time the name is written with a u. The census leaves the B unexpanded, and a school register would use the w again. The surname that applies to him here is Douglas, and the word in the relationship column is “Son.”

There was a boarder too, a tailor of twenty-five from Caithness. Lizzie appears as “Wife.” The census asked how long her present marriage had lasted, how many children had been born alive to that marriage, and how many of those children were still living. Eleven years, two born alive, two living. A reader can count the two children on the page. The form did not ask Lizzie to name the children behind those figures, and I cannot do that on her behalf.

What I can follow is the way the family identified one another over the next eighteen years. When the little boy started school in Dunfermline, the register named Robert Douglas as his guardian and used the word “Adopted.” When Laurence crossed the Atlantic in 1929, it was Janet, by then Mrs. Crombie, who traveled with him. Her husband was the relative he was going to in Chicago.

The passenger papers also asked whom he was leaving behind. By then Lizzie used the surname Anderson and lived at 39 Grieve Street in Dunfermline. To an official trying to identify his nearest relative in Scotland, Laurence gave the woman’s address and the name she went by then. For her relationship to him, he gave one word. Mother.

The 1911 census at 16 Lochrin Place, Edinburgh.
Sources and record notes
  1. Liberton statutory births, 1874, 693/70, p. 24, entry 70. Elizabeth Miller McDonald, May 31. Her age in April 1911 is calculated from this record. The age numeral in the family’s copy of the census is indistinct.
  2. Edinburgh St Giles, statutory marriages, 1899, 685/4 213. Parties, occupations, addresses and Janet Page Moodie as witness.
  3. 1901 census index, 5 Beaumont Place, schedule 24. Lizzie, Robert and eleven-month-old Janet.
  4. 1911 census, 16 Lochrin Place. The page uses the surname ditto mark. “B” alone is written, and the fertility columns have figures only.
  5. Queen Anne school register, entry 120, with the annotation “Adopted.”
  6. 1929 Duchess of Bedford passenger manifest, both pages. The continuation names Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson of 39 Grieve Street.

chapters.label: Chapter 13
chapters.title: Agnes Marries
chapters.html:
Four months after the census found her son in Lochrin Place, Agnes Brown gave an Edinburgh registrar another address. She was twenty-five, working as an asylum nurse. Her usual residence was West House, Royal Asylum, Morningside. The man beside her entry was twenty-one-year-old Thomas McKay McKenzie, an attendant at the same institution. In the space for Agnes’s residence the clerk could write “Same place.”

On Monday, August 28, 1911, they married at 34 Chambers Street. The marriage was by declaration in the presence of witnesses. Their record preserves both men’s names and what they did for a living. Edward Thomson was an asylum attendant, as Thomas was. John McIntyre was a coachman. A warrant of the Sheriff-Substitute of the Lothians and Peebles bears that day’s date. The entry was registered in Edinburgh that same day.

A couple on the preceding line had done much the same thing two days earlier. William Blackhall worked at the Royal Hotel as a hotel boots. Margaret Bruce was a tweed winder from Hawick. They too made their declaration at 34 Chambers Street. Their witnesses were a pattern weaver and his wife. On Saturday the hotel worker and the tweed winder stood before their witnesses. On Monday the attendant and the nurse did the same. Both couples left the names of the people who stood with them.

The marriage register brings Agnes’s parents back onto a page together. She gave her father as George Brown, a farm grieve, and her mother as Christina Brown, maiden surname Henderson. Both were deceased. Thomas’s father was John Alexander McKenzie, a coastguardsman. His mother, Mary McKay, had also died. The bride’s full name, as entered here, was Agnes McGarth Brown. Four years earlier the name attached to her son’s birth had been simply Agnes Brown. At the foot of both entries is the same registrar’s name, R. D. Robertson.

On May 6, 1912, at ten o’clock in the morning, Agnes had a daughter at 9 Stewart Terrace in Edinburgh. Thomas reported the birth on May 21. They called her Mary Christina McKenzie. Mary was the name of the sister who had shared Agnes’s grandmother’s house and then her uncle’s cottage. It was also the name of Thomas’s mother. Christina was the name of the mother Agnes had lost at five. Whatever the parents said to one another when they chose it, their daughter’s name carried something recognizable to both sides of the family.

Thomas later supplied his family particulars for the Army. On his service paper the children are Mary, born May 6, 1912, and Jean, born August 14, 1914, both in Edinburgh. His wife and next of kin was Agnes McKenzie. The Edinburgh address, 62 Balcarres Street, is crossed out. Below it someone entered Sherwood, Bonnyrigg, Midlothian. That correction gives us another place to follow her.

Mary and Jean were my grandfather’s younger half-sisters. When Mary was born, he was four and living with the Douglas family by the last account we have of him. Three months later, in a school register across the Forth, his name would be entered again. I have a father’s record of the two girls’ birthdays and the school’s record of their brother’s. Whether the three children were ever told one another’s names is a question those families left to ours.

Sources and record notes
  1. Edinburgh St Giles, statutory marriages, 1911, 685/04 0616, p. 308. Both declarations, witnesses, occupations, warrant and registrar are on the same page.
  2. Edinburgh Morningside, statutory births, 1912, 685/6 456. Mary Christina’s parents, birth, marriage particulars and informant.
  3. Thomas McKenzie, British Army descriptive report on enlistment. Next of kin, overwritten address and daughters’ births.

chapters.label: Chapter 14
chapters.title: Lawrence Douglas
chapters.html:
The family was still in Edinburgh in April 1911. By August of the following year, the Queen Anne school registers place the Douglas children across the Forth at Dunfermline. Somewhere between those records they moved house.

Their new address was 36 Victoria Terrace. It is a name worth keeping because it appears in two school entries only two days apart, one for a child who had been in school for years and the other for a boy starting for the first time.

On Monday, August 19, 1912, the Queen Anne Infant School in Dunfermline admitted a boy named Lawrence Douglas. The register gives his date of birth as June 14, 1907. He was five. The register lists no previous school.

Robert Douglas appears in the space for the boy's parent or guardian. His address was 36 Victoria Terrace. Beside it, in the column asking how the child was related to him, someone wrote a single word. Adopted.

The entry has a number, 120. A reader working down the left-hand page sees his name, birth date, Robert’s name and the home address. The qualification about how Robert and the boy were related sits across the opening. A transcription of only the first page could give a family almost everything it wanted and leave out the single word we had spent years looking for.

It is more than I had learned from the census. On the census the word beside him had been “Son.” Here was someone putting on paper that he had come into the family by adoption. The Scottish law that provided for adoption by court order was still eighteen years away. The school was recording the relationship in its own register.

Five years after a registrar in Edinburgh wrote Lawrence Brown, a school clerk in Dunfermline wrote Lawrence Douglas. The first name was spelled the way his mother had registered it. The surname was the one he would later give his own children.

Two days later, on August 21, the primary department entered Janet Douglas in its own register. She was twelve. She had come from the Commercial School. Her address was also 36 Victoria Terrace, and her guardian was Robert.

Seven years separated the children. For Janet there was an earlier school to put in the proper column. For Lawrence there was none. They had come to the same school, from the same home, and they would still be giving each other's names to officials on the other side of the Atlantic seventeen years later.

Queen Anne Infant School. Admission 120, August 19, 1912.
Sources and record notes
  1. Queen Anne Infant School, entry 120. Date, birth date, guardian, domicile and annotation on the facing page.
  2. Queen Anne Primary School, Janet Douglas. Same guardian and address.
  3. National Records of Scotland, adoption and private arrangements before 1930.

chapters.label: Chapter 15
chapters.title: A Boy in Dunfermline
chapters.html:
My grandfather’s first school in Dunfermline was Queen Anne. At 36 Victoria Terrace there were two Douglas children to send to school that August, and their entries survive in different books. The infant register puts Lawrence in a class of children just beginning. In the primary register his twelve-year-old sister already had a school history of her own. Next to Janet’s name was the name of the school she had come from, Commercial.

Someone at the school took down his exact birthday, June 14, 1907. On the facing page, under the question about a guardian’s relationship to the child, someone wrote “Adopted.” It is a small entry among the names of other children arriving that summer. One had come from Glasgow, another from Townhill. A few lines above Laurence there was a child whose guardian was an aunt. The school needed to know which adult answered for each child. For both Douglas children, the name was Robert Douglas and the address was the same.

Dunfermline stood on high ground north of the Forth. Linen weaving had made a living here long before the coming of the steam mills. Andrew Carnegie, the town’s famous emigrant, had been born the son of a handloom weaver. As a boy he had left Dunfermline for Pennsylvania. By the time Laurence started school there, a child could grow up among things Carnegie had given back to the town. Pittencrieff, the glen at the foot of the hill by the abbey, had become a public park through his gift in 1903. Up in the town stood the first of his public library buildings.

There was a family occasion behind that library. When Carnegie came home for the laying of its foundation stone in July 1881, it was his mother who laid it. The library opened in 1883. Over the entrance were the words “Let There Be Light.” My family remembers that my grandfather loved to read. I have often wondered what books he got hold of as a boy. His school and street are known to us. The titles he would have recognized on a shelf are among the things I wish somebody had asked him.

Janet’s schooldays ended on August 1, 1914. The register gave the reason in two words, “Age 14.” Three days later Britain entered the war. Laurence was seven. Down by the Forth the Admiralty had been building a dockyard at Rosyth. By December British battlecruisers were based in the Forth. For a boy in Dunfermline, the places named in naval news included the stretch of water between his school town and the city where he had been born.

On January 11, 1916, Laurence moved up to the primary department at Queen Anne. He was eight. His entry, number 1191, again names Robert as guardian. It also gives us the next address at which we can place him, 5 Foundry Street. The dates tell us when the school had the addresses. The family’s moving day lies somewhere between them.

That spring, the war reached both shores. On the night of April 2–3 a German airship raided Edinburgh and Leith. Among the streets hit was Lauriston Place. Then, on May 30, the battlecruisers sailed from the Forth. The fighting off Jutland lasted from May 31 into June 1. HMS Queen Mary and HMS Indefatigable were among the British ships lost. My grandfather would turn nine a fortnight later. He had been eight when bombs fell on the Edinburgh street where Agnes gave birth to him. He was still eight when the ships that survived Jutland came home to the Forth.

Sources and record notes
  1. Queen Anne Infant School, admission 120, August 19, 1912. Compare the facing page for guardianship and previous schools.
  2. Janet Douglas, Queen Anne Primary register. Admission August 21, 1912, previous school and leaving entry August 1, 1914.
  3. Lawrence Douglas, Queen Anne Primary register, entry 1191, January 11, 1916, Robert at 5 Foundry Street.
  4. Dunfermline Heritage Community Projects, Your Guide to Dunfermline, Carnegie Library. The family’s recollection concerns Laurence’s love of reading. His borrowing history is unknown.
  5. Carnegie Corporation, The Carnegie Dunfermline Trust, origins and gift of Pittencrieff.
  6. National Records of Scotland, Battle of Jutland 1916, fleet bases, battle dates and losses.
  7. Scottish Archives for Schools, Attacks from the Air, contemporary Edinburgh records of the April raid.

chapters.label: Chapter 16
chapters.title: Fire Over Edinburgh
chapters.html:
On Sunday, April 2, 1916, German airships set out across the North Sea. One of them reached the Forth late that night. There was a dockyard at Rosyth and a railway bridge across the water. Down in the streets of Leith and Edinburgh, the places actually struck could be identified afterward, one address at a time.

The airship that came up the Forth was L 14. Its commander was Alois Böcker. Edinburgh had already received its warning. Lights had been lowered and traffic stopped. Around half past eleven the first bombs fell on Leith. The Leith chief constable’s account begins at Edinburgh Dock. A bomb also struck the bonded whisky warehouse of Innes and Grieve. The chief constable traced the damage street by street.

The airship then crossed into Edinburgh. A bomb struck the house of Doctor John McLaren at 39 Lauriston Place. Part of the roof and a wall came away. The McLaren family escaped injury. In nearby Graham Street, David Robertson, a young gunner already invalided out of the army, was struck by a fragment and later died at the Royal Infirmary. At 79 Lauriston Place stood the Royal Maternity Hospital.

At 16 Marshall Street the blast killed John Smith, a tinsmith, and his fifteen-year-old son, William. The valuation roll for the year before the raid gives that address as their home. Another man killed there was David T. Graham. His brother verified the occupation on his death certificate. David was a chief cinema attendant. Alongside the street addresses in the damage reports, we have a son’s age, a father’s trade and the occupation one brother gave for another.

In his report of April 12 the chief constable of Leith accounted for twenty explosive and incendiary bombs in his district. His report went from the Town Hall to the Scottish Office in Whitehall. Edinburgh kept its own evidence. The city’s photographic collections preserve a view of the damage. Its catalogue identifies Lauriston Place, the Grassmarket and Marshall Street among the places struck. The paper trail extends far beyond the brief time the airship was overhead.

Thomas McKenzie had given the Army an Edinburgh address for Agnes on his enlistment papers. Across the water in Dunfermline, Laurence's January school entry gives the address on Foundry Street. I don't know what either of them saw that night. I do know that the house hit on Lauriston Place stood on the very street where Agnes had given birth to him.

Sources and record notes
  1. Leith chief constable’s report and accompanying archive resources, April 1916.
  2. Edinburgh Libraries, After the 1916 Zeppelin Raid, contemporary photograph and catalogue.
  3. Ian Castle, April 2/3, 1916, flight and casualties. The chapter’s family addresses come from the January 1916 school register and McKenzie service papers.
  4. Thomas McKenzie’s military attestation and next-of-kin information.
  5. Edinburgh Libraries, History of the house: Nicolson Square and Marshall Street. The Smith family in the census and valuation roll, and David T. Graham’s occupation on his death certificate.

chapters.label: Chapter 17
chapters.title: The House on Foundry Street
chapters.html:
On September 9, 1919, Lizzie Douglas gave a registrar in Edinburgh the address of her family in Dunfermline. She had come into the record as a widow. Robert had died at Woodburn Sanatorium on Canaan Lane, across the Forth from their house on Foundry Street.

The death entry gives two conditions with different histories. Beside pulmonary tuberculosis the doctor entered about a year. Beside lupus the duration went back to childhood. The certifying physician was Isabella Mears. The name in the informant’s column was Elizabeth Douglas.

The hour of his death was half past seven in the morning. He was forty-three. His trade was entered as stone machineman. That same day Elizabeth Douglas reported the death. She gave her address as 5 Foundry Street, Dunfermline, and signed as his widow.

Lizzie was forty-five. Laurence was twelve years old.

A year later, on October 8, 1920, the education authority granted him an exemption that allowed him to leave school before the usual age of fourteen. The register records the reason in four words: "Granted Exemption by E.A." The entry gives a date. It says nothing about his first day's work or what arrangements his mother made. By the following summer, all three members of the family had jobs.

The census was taken on June 19, 1921, five days after Laurence turned fourteen. Lizzie, forty-seven, was now head of the house and was cleaning schools for the Fife Education Authority. Janet, twenty-one, was a clerk with the Dunfermline Co-operative Society. Laurence was a message boy for McClelland and Company, a grocer. A saleswoman named Margaret Dobson boarded with them. The four of them had three rooms with windows, the measure used on the Scottish return. For Margaret, the form gives her age as thirty-seven years and six months. The amount of detail is remarkable in a household from which no letter about ordinary working life has come down to us.

For children under fifteen the census asked whether either parent had died. Beside Laurence's name the answer was abbreviated to two letters, meaning father dead. I know the name of the man his school had entered as his guardian, the man whose death Lizzie registered. He was Robert Douglas.

When Laurence sailed in 1929, he still gave the grocery trade as his occupation. There are eight years between the message boy on the census and the grocer on the passenger list. I cannot name all his employers in those years. The first one I can name is the firm that took on a child from Foundry Street before his fifteenth birthday.

The Douglas household at 5 Foundry Street in the 1921 census.
Sources and record notes
  1. Morningside deaths, 685/6 1161, registered September 9, 1919. Pulmonary tuberculosis and lupus are separately listed. No causal connection between them is asserted.
  2. Queen Anne Primary register, October 8, 1920, leaving entry.
  3. 1921 Dunfermline census, schedule 116. Room count, occupations, employers and orphanhood column.

chapters.label: Chapter 18
chapters.title: Janet Sails First
chapters.html:
Before my grandfather had a Chicago address, his sister had one. Her full name was Janet Page Douglas. Queen Anne recorded her as Janet Douglas. In the American files where I found her again she was Janet Crombie. She was the first of the two children raised at Foundry Street to make the crossing, and she left enough of a trail for her brother to follow three years later.

When the Scottish census was taken on June 19, 1921, Janet was twenty-one. Her occupation at 5 Foundry Street was entered as clerkess, her employer the Dunfermline Co-operative Society. Her mother Lizzie, widowed by then, cleaned schools for the Fife Education Authority. Her brother had turned fourteen five days earlier. Beside his name the census gives his job as message boy for a grocer, McClelland & Co. The fourth person in the household was Margaret Dobson, a boarder, who worked as a saleswoman. The return counted three rooms with windows and gave an occupation for each of the four people. That is the last census I have of Janet as an unmarried daughter at home.

On Friday, July 16, 1926, she married Thomas Crombie in Dunfermline. She was twenty-six. Two separate American citizenship petitions preserve that Scottish date. Years later in Chicago, when each spouse had to give the particulars of the marriage, Janet and Thomas both gave July 16 and both gave Dunfermline. There is a difference between reading a marriage entry and reading two people’s later sworn accounts of their own wedding. Here we have the latter, and they agree.

Less than two months after the wedding, on September 13, Janet entered the United States at Detroit. The route into the country was by rail from Canada. Her papers identify the Canadian Pacific. She supplied the American border date when she applied to become a citizen. It is a much firmer point in her story than any day one might choose for the opening of a trunk or a goodbye at a Scottish door.

The United States records eventually supply what the Scottish school register could never have given us, the name and address by which an adult brother could find his sister in another country. In September 1929 Thomas Crombie was the Chicago relative named in Laurence’s passenger papers, his address on South Kostner Avenue. Janet was traveling with Laurence that time. The 1930 Chicago census gives Thomas’s occupation as a furniture salesman and calls Laurence his brother-in-law.

Janet’s own journey had made the later crossing possible in one quite specific sense. When Laurence was asked for a person he was going to, there was a person to name. On one side of the Atlantic he could give officials his mother’s address in Dunfermline. On the other he could give them his sister’s married family in Chicago. In a family history that loses him altogether for a stretch of his childhood, his older sister becomes the person by whom I can follow him from one country to the other.

Sources and record notes
  1. Dunfermline census, 1921, 424/1 ED 12, schedule 116. The return records the four occupants, their work and the three-room count.
  2. Janet Crombie, United States naturalization petition 329111. Her own account of marriage and admission at Detroit.
  3. Thomas Crombie, United States naturalization petition 327632, front. Independent statement by the other spouse.
  4. Duchess of Bedford passenger list, 1929, for the family on each side of the Atlantic.
  5. 1930 Chicago census, ED 16-834. The Crombie household continues onto the next sheet, where the relationship is brother-in-law.

chapters.label: Chapter 19
chapters.title: Last Days in Scotland
chapters.html:
In the spring of 1929 Janet came home.

On May 18, 1929, the Canadian Pacific liner Montroyal landed at Greenock from Quebec. Among the third-class passengers was Janet Crombie, twenty-nine, married, housewife. Her permanent home was in the United States. For her address in Britain she gave 39 Grieve Street, Dunfermline. In September, both Janet and Laurence would give that same Grieve Street address for their mother, Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson. I have yet to find the first record in which Lizzie used the name Anderson.

There is an undated photograph identified in family collections as Janet and Laurence with ice-cream cones. They stand beside an iron railing in front of a pale wall. Janet is small and neat in a long coat with big round buttons, her dark hair bobbed with a fringe. She holds one cone near her mouth and another in her other hand. He is much taller than she is, leaning against the railing with one knee bent. His hair is combed straight back. His jacket is open over a sweater and tie, and there is a light-colored handkerchief in his breast pocket. My family remembers how carefully he dressed. Here, even with an ice-cream cone in his hand, he is wearing a tie.

I do not have a date or a place for the picture. I like it because in the official records these two are usually schoolchildren, workers, passengers or relatives at an address. Here they are a sister and a brother eating ice cream.

By September 1929 he had his papers for America. He was twenty-two, a grocer by trade. Immigration records described him as about six feet tall, fair-haired and blue-eyed.

On September 3, the American consulate at Glasgow issued his visa, number 27768. He had been Douglas at school and Douglas at the grocer's on the census. On his travel papers he is Brown again, the surname Agnes had given him at birth. The American papers spell his first name Lawrence, with a w. The British list spells it Laurence.

I don't know when Laurence learned about Agnes, or what he knew of her when he sailed. What I can say is that he was twenty-two, his mother in Dunfermline was the woman he called Elizabeth Anderson, and he was booked to sail on the same ship as his sister. Four days after the visa was issued, they sailed.

chapters.label: Chapter 20
chapters.title: The Crossing
chapters.html:
On Saturday, September 7, 1929, the Duchess of Bedford sailed from Greenock. The ship belonged to Canadian Pacific. She was new, built the year before at Clydebank by John Brown and Company, with a black hull, white upperworks and two funnels. My grandfather went out of Scotland on a ship built on the river from which he sailed.

The British list of passengers leaving the country shows Janet Crombie and Laurence Brown in cabin class. The ship's master was H. Sibbons. Its contracted landing was Montreal. Photographs of the ship from 1928 show a dining saloon on A deck, an observation room on the promenade deck and small three-berth cabins.

On the American list, filled in before the ship arrived, he gave his particulars: Lawrence Brown, twenty-two, single, grocer, born in Edinburgh, last residence Dunfermline. For his nearest relative in Scotland, he named his mother, Mrs. Elizabeth Anderson, at 39 Grieve Street. For the person he was going to in America, he named his brother-in-law, Thomas Crombie, at 1534 South Kostner Avenue in Chicago.

The ship came up the St. Lawrence and reached Quebec on Friday, September 13. A doctor of the United States Public Health Service examined him at Quebec and stamped his papers as passed.

Two days later, on Sunday, September 15, an American immigration inspector recorded his admission at Detroit. The border card gives a description of him that a daughter or a grandchild can still read. About six feet tall. Fair hair. Fair complexion. Blue eyes. Occupation, grocer.

He had paid his own passage. He had fifty dollars and had never been in the United States before. He gave his reason for coming as seeking work. For the length of time he meant to stay, the inspector wrote "permanent."

One form, filled out for an American inspector, holds quite a bit of our family. The passenger's own surname was Brown. The mother he left behind was Anderson. The man he was going to was Crombie. The relationship between them all runs through the Douglas household in which he and Janet grew up.

We have always understood that the pocket watch my grandmother gave me came across with him. That part of the crossing comes to me from home. The name on his Detroit entry card is Lawrence Brown.

He went on to Chicago that autumn. On October 29, a little over six weeks after his admission at Detroit, Wall Street had the trading day that became known as Black Tuesday.

Three places on the passenger and admission papers

Greenock, September 7, 1929. Janet Crombie and Laurence Brown on the British outward list. Quebec, September 13. Medical examination on arrival. Detroit, September 15. Entry under Lawrence Brown, with Chicago as his destination.

The Canadian Pacific liner Duchess of Bedford. Date of this photograph unknown.

chapters.label: Chapter 21
chapters.title: Chicago
chapters.html:
Chicago in 1930 was a city of more than three million people, the second largest in the country.

The first American census in which my grandfather appears is the one taken that spring. To find him you have to turn the page. Near the bottom of one sheet on South Kostner Avenue in Chicago are Thomas and Janet Crombie. They paid thirty-two dollars a month in rent. At the top of the next sheet is Lawrence Brown, twenty-two, Thomas's brother-in-law. Thomas sold furniture. Laurence was a salesman in a grocery. He had brought his trade across the ocean with him.

The census gives the house number on South Kostner as 1532. On his way into the country the previous September, Laurence had given 1534. I kept both readings. The name Brown alone would make him hard to pick out in an Illinois grocery. The people he lived with, and the words brother-in-law on the continuation sheet, identify the family.

At home in Dunfermline he had appeared beside Janet as a Douglas. On the ship they had traveled as Janet Crombie and Laurence Brown. Here in Chicago a stranger reading down the two census sheets could have missed their connection entirely. The question on the form was how each person was related to the head of the household. Its answer on the line for Lawrence Brown takes us back across the page to Thomas and, through him, to Janet.

The line for Lawrence is numbered 51. The enumerator entered 1929 as the year he came to America, the same year stamped on the card at Detroit. In Dunfermline he had been a message boy for McClelland and Company. In Chicago he was selling groceries. Those two records give me something of his working life on both sides of the Atlantic. The Chicago sheet gives his trade and leaves his employer unnamed.

In October 1934 Elizabeth Anderson appeared in the immigration records as a housekeeper of sixty from Dunfermline. She had sailed to Quebec. She gave her daughter Janet as the person she was joining. Her destination was 1518 South Kostner Avenue, on the same street her son had named five years before. Lizzie's own card puts her journey in the family story. Whether and when she and Laurence saw each other again is something I would still like to know.

Laurence later gave Chicago as his home in the spring of 1935. On October 3, 1936, Janet had twin daughters there, Elizabeth and Jessie. Janet and Thomas both gave the girls’ names and birthdays in their citizenship papers. My grandfather was twenty-nine when he became their uncle. I cannot place him in Chicago for their birth. The next city directory in which I can trace his trade was published in Providence.

Chicago, 1930. Lawrence Brown on the continuation of the Crombie household.
Elizabeth Anderson’s immigration card, October 1934.

chapters.label: Chapter 22
chapters.title: Weybosset Street
chapters.html:
Providence, Rhode Island, was an old, compact city of brick and granite at the head of Narragansett Bay, built on textile mills and the jewelry trade. In the 1930s its downtown was the shopping center for the whole state. Westminster Street and Weybosset Street ran side by side, a block apart, lined with department stores, specialty shops, banks and theaters. At the heart of it stood the Outlet Company, the city's great department store.

In the Providence directory for 1937 there is a short entry for Lawrence Douglas. The business address was 165 Weybosset Street. He lived at 35 Elmwood Avenue, in an apartment building called The Arches. His occupation was display manager.

The address on Weybosset belonged to the John Mason Building, a six-story steel-framed building put up in 1903, across the street from the Outlet. The street listings for 1937 and 1938 put Bond Stores, a clothing chain, at number 165. The matching name and trade identify him provisionally. Laurence would later name Bond Stores as his employer, and a census taker would describe his trade as window trimmer in retail clothing.

A city directory distinguishes the address where a man earned money from the one where he went home. In display work the distinction has an unusually visible form. People could walk past the result of the day’s work on a downtown sidewalk without ever knowing the name of the man responsible. In Providence the directory gives us that man’s trade. In San Francisco the draft card would give both his workplace and his signature.

His family remembered his own appearance. His hair was carefully combed and his clothes were well kept. In the photograph with Janet you can even see the handkerchief folded into his jacket pocket. The picture and the recollection tell me something about the man who dressed the windows. They give me no way of knowing who taught him the trade or what his first window looked like.

The following year the directory still lists him at 165 Weybosset. By then his home address was 459 Pine Street. Across two years, with two places to live, the work address held steady.

Across Weybosset Street, the Outlet Company occupied numbers 168 through 176. Its sales floor faced the sidewalk through large display windows. The Mason Building opposite had space for shops and offices. Stone, Carpenter & Willson designed it for the John N. Mason Real Estate Company. Someone looking for my grandfather’s place of work on a street plan can put a finger on the right block, between those two buildings.

In the 1937 directory, another entry gives a woman's name and a place of work just one street away. She was a hairdresser at 290 Westminster. Her workplace and his were a few minutes' walk apart. Her name was Constance Darcy.
