chapters.label: Chapter 23
chapters.title: Constance
chapters.html:
The first place I can put my grandmother is 410 Smith Street in Providence. Her name fills a line in the city’s birth register for Saturday, October 12, 1912. Constance Eugenie Darcy, first child. Her father was Albert B. Darcy, a twenty-three-year-old printer born in East Providence. Her mother was eighteen and came from Canada. Across the Atlantic, the boy she would marry had started school in Dunfermline less than eight weeks before.

Her parents had married in Providence on January 16 of that year. On their marriage entry he is Albert Blake Darcy and she is Eugenie Emma Delaire, seventeen, born in Sutton, Quebec. On her daughter’s birth entry the spelling of her name is Eugenia. Her parents appear on the marriage entry as Timothy and Julia M. Delaire. William Pyne officiated. The Providence directory for 1913 brings Julia Delaire, widowed, to 410 Smith Street as a boarder. Albert is listed there too. That is the same address Constance’s parents had given at her birth the previous October. That old directory, meant to help people find one another in the city, gives our family a house with three generations to its name.

A second child came on December 7, 1915, in Taunton, Massachusetts. They named him Albert Norman Darcy. When his father registered for the draft in June 1917, he was working for the Pawtucket Times. He listed the people dependent on him as his wife, two children and his mother-in-law. Julia can disappear from a family story if all we have to go on is her daughter’s married name. Albert’s own account of the people he supported puts her back in it.

Albert made his living on the production side of a newspaper. A linotype operator sat at a keyboard. Pressing a letter key released a little brass matrix bearing that character. When the line was ready, the machine cast it in hot metal. The printer could lift out a solid line of type carrying the words someone else would read in the paper. Albert went on to work for the Providence Journal. Many years later, in March 1961, the Pawtucket Times carried a notice identifying his daughter as the widow of Laurence Douglas. One of the papers her father had helped put into type had become a source for the history of her own family.

The children spent part of their early lives on Alms Street in Providence. The 1920 census lists Constance, seven, and Albert, four, with both parents. Five years later the state census places the family in East Providence. By 1930 Eugenie headed a rented household at 111 Pratt Street back in Providence. The rent was twenty-eight dollars a month. She gave her occupation as decorator in a rug works. Constance, seventeen, was still at school. Her brother was fourteen.

For several years we can watch Constance make her way into a trade in her own name. The 1934 directory calls her a student at 7 Beacon Avenue. A Rhode Island state census card dated January 6, 1936, carries a different address, 75 Abbott Street. The card asks for both her usual and her present occupation. The answer to both is hairdresser.

In 1937 the Providence directory gives her workplace as 290 Westminster Street, room 506, and her home as 11 Grand View. The following year the printed address reads “290 Wash rm 402.” I can make out the number and room, but I have kept the street as the directory printed it. Elsewhere in that same volume, Anton’s beauty shop is listed at 290 Westminster, room 402. The matching room is a clue to the address. The entries give me no basis for naming her employer. Her home address that year was 56 Dartmouth Avenue. Her mother and younger brother appear there too. Even after my grandmother had an occupation and a business address of her own, there is still a door in the records through which all three of them passed.

The same directories list a Lawrence Douglas doing display work at 165 Weybosset Street. The name and the trade fit my grandfather. The two listings lead me into the same downtown Providence my family knew, to a hairdresser’s room and a display manager’s place of business. I have never found the story of the day they met. What my family remembers of Constance is how easy she was to be with. A directory can give me the room where she worked. That last detail I have from the people who loved her.

chapters.label: Chapter 24
chapters.title: The Hurricane of 1938
chapters.html:
On Wednesday, September 21, 1938, a hurricane drove water up Narragansett Bay and into downtown Providence.

Four days of rain had already swollen rivers in New England. Out in the Atlantic the hurricane was moving north with extraordinary speed. It crossed Long Island that afternoon and came ashore again in Connecticut near high tide. What happened in Providence depended as much on the shape of the bay as on the path of the storm.

Downtown Providence stood at the narrow end of Narragansett Bay. As the wind drove water north, the narrowing shore channeled it toward the downtown shopping district where their workplaces appear in the directories.

On Weybosset Street, across from the Outlet department store, was the building the directories list for the display manager Lawrence Douglas. Where he and Constance were that afternoon, no record I have found says. To see what the day was like, there are people who lived through it and told their own stories afterward.

One of them was Loraine Martin, who was to marry Josef Fogel that evening at the Narragansett Hotel on Dorrance Street. Miss Dyer, the society editor of The Providence Journal, telephoned to ask if the wedding would go ahead. Loraine told her it would. The PBS documentary The Hurricane of '38 says the bridegroom spent hours stranded at Union Station.

By midafternoon the wind was tearing through Rhode Island. Doris Layden, riding downtown with her father, saw the front window of a furniture store come out. She remembered the glass breaking as the wind carried it along the street. Doris could name something she and her father had seen together. The broken window belongs to her account of the storm.

Along the shore in Westerly, the storm surge swept away summer cottages. Farther up the bay the water passed the islands and entered the Providence River. The city was in the path of water gathered along miles of open shore.

It reached downtown at about five o'clock, as office workers and shoppers were starting home. In Exchange Place, in front of City Hall, the water rose from a few inches deep to waist high in minutes. It ran up Weybosset Street and through the doors of the shops. Loraine saw parked cars swept along Dorrance Street toward the river. As the water reached the wiring of the flooded cars, their horns began to sound. Years afterward, Doris Layden still remembered hearing those horns through the water. The wind gauge at the Weather Bureau recorded eighty-seven miles an hour. At the Biltmore Hotel, people threw bedsheets from the second floor for those caught in the current to grab.

When the water crested at Market Square, it stood thirteen feet eight and a half inches above mean high water. A bronze plaque on the Market House records the height. It was nearly two feet higher than the mark left by the great gale of 1815, the worst flood the city had known until then.

By nightfall the water was draining back toward the bay. Downtown was dark. The National Guard began patrolling while the water was still receding. Photographs of the wreckage at Fox Point include the steamer Monhegan. Even with the water down, Providence had the storm on its streets and in its harbour.

The Fogels were married by candlelight. In their later recollections, they differed on how late the ceremony took place. Loraine also remembered the water pouring into shops on Weybosset Street. That was the street printed beside my grandfather’s trade in the Providence directory that year.

In August 1954 Hurricane Carol put downtown Providence under water again. By then Laurence and Constance were back in Rhode Island with their three daughters. The protection eventually built across the Providence River came too late for him to see. The Army Corps of Engineers dates the start of construction at Fox Point to July 1961, four months after he died. The barrier was completed in January 1966.

  2. American Experience, The Hurricane of ’38, oral histories of Loraine Martin Fogel, Josef Fogel and Doris Layden.

  4. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Fox Point Hurricane Protection Barrier. Construction July 1961 to January 1966.

chapters.label: Chapter 25
chapters.title: A Wedding in Alabama
chapters.html:
On February 10, 1939, a daughter was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts. Laurence gave the date and birthplace when he named his children in his American citizenship papers. Her name was Eugenie Elizabeth. There was an Eugenie on her mother’s side of the family, the Quebec-born grandmother whose name Constance herself carried. There was an Elizabeth on her father’s side, the woman who had raised him in Scotland. Both names that the little girl would carry in America were already familiar in her parents’ families.

On Monday, October 9, Laurence and Constance married in Birmingham, Alabama. It was three days before her twenty-seventh birthday. He was thirty-two. At first glance there is very little in the places we knew them by that would lead anyone to Jefferson County. He had been born in Edinburgh and she in Providence. Their daughter had been born in Massachusetts. On the marriage application Laurence supplied a Chicago address for himself and a Providence one for his bride.

His was 1860 South Hamlin Avenue. The following year the Chicago census would find his sister Janet and her husband Thomas Crombie at that address. The Providence address was 454 Broadway. For a couple standing on an Alabama record, the particulars reach a remarkable distance. One address takes us back to the sister who crossed the Atlantic with him. The other puts Constance in the city where I can follow her from the day she was born.

The name on the groom’s line was Lawrence Douglas. He gave his occupation as salesman. The form asked who his parents were. Robert Douglas, he said, and Elizabeth McDonald. More than thirty years had gone by since Agnes Brown had stood as the mother on his Edinburgh birth entry. In Birmingham, the two people he chose to identify for his own marriage record were the man who had answered for him at school and the woman he had called his mother when he sailed. In the space for Constance’s parents he gave Albert B. Darcy and Eugenie Delaire. The bride’s name was entered as Constance Darcy. Laurence signed as the person supplying the particulars for them both.

The page in the Jefferson County book holds more than the couple’s names. The application is where I find the addresses, the occupations and the names of the parents. The bond and the certificate are on the same page. It is the certificate that places the wedding itself in Birmingham on October 9. The distinction matters for a couple who gave home addresses in two other states.

The Alabama marriage papers also identify the man who married Laurence and Constance. Thomas R. Lea was a municipal court judge. The certificate records his part in the ceremony and leaves the witness lines blank. Newspaper indexes place their names in two Birmingham papers the next day, the Post and the Age-Herald. Those newspaper references give us a place to look for how the city reported the event. The marriage record itself answers the question of when and by whom they were married.

I have yet to learn why they chose Birmingham. Six months later they were keeping house together on Valencia Street in San Francisco, with a one-year-old daughter born in Massachusetts. When Laurence was asked about his marriage again in Pennsylvania, he gave the bride’s family name, Darcy, and once again he supplied October 9, 1939, and Birmingham. That is how a single day in Alabama became part of the story of the family my mother grew up in.

chapters.label: Chapter 26
chapters.title: San Francisco
chapters.html:
By the spring of 1940, Laurence and Constance had crossed the country and come to San Francisco.

In April 1940 their home was in the Mission District. The census page records Valencia Street. On their line the space for the house number is empty. I can take the family to that street in the spring of 1940 and put a figure on the rent they paid there.

On April 11, 1940, a census taker came to Valencia Street in the Mission. The Douglas family paid thirty-three dollars a month in rent. Laurence worked in a clothing store. The words used for his trade were window trimmer. He had worked forty-eight hours in the week the census asked about. For the whole of the previous year he reported earnings of two thousand two hundred and forty dollars.

The census asked where each person had lived five years earlier. For Laurence the answer was Chicago. For Constance it was Providence. Their daughter was one year old. The three birthplaces in the household were Scotland, Rhode Island and Massachusetts. Now the three of them lived in California.

His employer was Bond Stores, one of the largest men's clothing chains in America, founded in Cleveland in 1914. The San Francisco store stood at Post and Kearny streets, two blocks from Union Square. The 1941 city directory lists him as a displayman at Bond Clothes, with his wife Constance.

In Europe the war went on. France fell that summer, and London was bombed through the autumn. The United States had yet to enter the war. Even so, on October 16, 1940, Laurence registered for the draft. The reverse of his card carries the stamp of Local Board 94. He gave a new address, 129 Julian Avenue. He named his employer, Bond Stores, at Post and Kearny. For the person who would always know where to reach him, he gave his wife, Constance. The card describes him as about six feet tall and 160 pounds, with blue eyes, and he signed it Laurence Brown Douglas.

It was in San Francisco that my mother was born. Her parents called her Constance Anderson Douglas. She had her mother's first name. Anderson was the name Laurence had used for Lizzie at the Canadian border. My mother's birthday is February 2. California's birth index gives the year as 1941. In his citizenship papers her father subsequently gave 1942. The month and day agree. For the year I have followed the California birth index.

In June 1941 Laurence and his wife went north into Canada. He had obtained a re-entry permit for the trip. On Saturday, June 21, they returned by motor coach at Blaine, Washington. The inspector put down his occupation as displayman, his age, his height of about six feet, his brown hair and blue eyes, and their San Francisco address on Mirabel Avenue. Brown is the description on this card. The one at Detroit had said fair. It was nearly twelve years since Laurence had first entered the country at Detroit with fifty dollars and the name of a brother-in-law in Chicago. Now he gave an address on the Pacific coast, and Constance was beside him.

The next day, Germany invaded the Soviet Union. Six months later, the war would reach America.

chapters.label: Chapter 27
chapters.title: The Night of the Sirens
chapters.html:
The last time I can put my grandparents together before America entered the war is on a border card. On June 21, 1941, Laurence returned to the United States at Blaine, Washington. The card says his wife Constance, an American citizen, was with him. Their destination was San Francisco. My family remembers a different arrangement by autumn. Laurence had gone east to the Pittsburgh district for work, and Constance was still in San Francisco.

Two men in Pennsylvania left a date that helps us follow the family account. David Hunter was a machinist and Frank Holliday a clerk. Each later swore that he had known my grandfather since September 1941. There were people who could account for him on the West Coast, too. When he applied for citizenship, the period for which the authorities sought evidence from San Francisco ran from February to September of that year. Across those papers and the family’s memory, September is the month that keeps coming back.

On Sunday, December 7, the first reports of the attack on Pearl Harbor reached San Francisco at about half past eleven in the morning. By one that afternoon people were volunteering at police and fire stations. At the Northern Police Station on Greenwich Street, 385 had lined up by half past three. The city needed to know what each could do. One volunteer, Hazel Shive, said she could drive a truck or work as a nurse. It is her name and her offer that survive in the newspaper account of that afternoon.

The alarms in San Francisco itself came the following day. At about a quarter past six on Monday evening, people began to hear warnings. Police cars sounded their sirens. Fire engines added theirs. A blackout required the people who could see a light to find somebody who could actually turn it off. Some of the hardest to extinguish were electric advertising signs on rooftops. They had been set on timers, and their controls were out of reach of the people below.

David Perlman was a young Chronicle reporter that December. Sent up to the roof of the newspaper building with binoculars, he saw a light in the sky and thought he had spotted a plane. It was a star. The newspaper’s front page the next morning counted four alarms. People in the streets on Monday evening had to decide what to do with the information available then. No bombs fell on San Francisco that night.

I have my family’s account of where my grandparents were that autumn. It does not give me a house in which to put Constance on December 8, or tell me when she and Laurence heard from one another. The city’s newspapers preserve the hours of the alarms, the places where people volunteered and even the mistake a reporter made on a roof. My grandmother’s whereabouts that Monday evening belong to her own, unrecorded part of the story.

The next address I can give for all four of them is 612 California Avenue. In spite of its name, the street was in Avalon, Pennsylvania, outside Pittsburgh. On February 11, 1943, Laurence listed Constance Darcy as his wife and gave the names of the two little girls living there, Eugenie Elizabeth and Constance Anderson. The younger girl was my mother. Her family remembered her parents in two different cities in the autumn of 1941. By February 1943 her father could give one address for them all.

chapters.label: Chapter 28
chapters.title: An American Citizen
chapters.html:
Laurence Brown Douglas was living at 612 California Avenue in Avalon, just outside Pittsburgh, when he petitioned for American citizenship. He was a display manager for Bond Stores. The papers describe him as five feet eleven, with blue eyes and brown hair. They give his date of birth as June 14, 1907. More than thirty-five years after Agnes registered him in Edinburgh, her son was giving the same date for himself in Pennsylvania.

His petition was numbered 139903. One of the questions took him back to his entrance into the country. He gave Detroit and September 15, 1929. The card made at Detroit survives. The younger man on it was single, with fifty dollars and a brother-in-law in Chicago. The man making the petition in Pennsylvania had a wife and children and a job with Bond Stores. He gave the authorities enough particulars to put the two records together.

Two men in the Pittsburgh area vouched for him on February 11, 1943. David Hunter was a machinist. Frank Holliday was a clerk. On March 3, two people who had known him in California gave depositions in San Francisco. Their names were William Howard Vahlkamp and Betty Johnstone Sherwood. His move across the country meant that some of the people able to speak for him lived more than two thousand miles away.

The California witnesses had known him in the city where he worked before moving east. Their depositions still belong to the same file as the evidence given in Pittsburgh. His neighbors and acquaintances had a part in the record he left my mother. They could speak about the months in which they saw him. His account of his birth, his marriage and the births of his daughters was his own.

He named his wife, Constance Darcy, and gave Birmingham as the place of their marriage. He listed Eugenie Elizabeth and Constance Anderson as his daughters. He also gave the date on which he had entered the United States at Detroit and the name he had used on entry. Lawrence Brown.

On May 6, 1943, he took the oath and was admitted as a citizen of the United States. On the record of that day his name is Laurence Brown Douglas. February 11 was the date of the petition and the Pittsburgh witnesses. March 3 was the date of the California testimony. The day he became a citizen was the Thursday in May.

It is one of the reasons I can tell my mother with confidence that the boy registered in Edinburgh, the young grocer who came through Detroit, and the man who raised her were the same person. On the citizenship papers he brought the names together himself.

chapters.label: Chapter 29
chapters.title: River Avenue
chapters.html:
By 1947 the family was back in Rhode Island. The Pawtucket directory gives their address as 97 Magill Street. Laurence was dressing windows. In Providence by 1950, he and Constance were living at 148 General Street. They remained in the directories there for several years. The 1956 Providence directory lists them at 644 River Avenue. Laurence and Constance rented the house on River Avenue, as they did every home they lived in together.

Constance is named beside him in the Pawtucket directory. The shift from Magill Street to General Street is one I can trace in city books whose compilers were simply keeping track of the people who lived and worked among their customers. Entries survive for the years in which an American census would leave us waiting a decade. Those entries help me place the girls’ childhood on three streets, first Magill in Pawtucket, then General and River in Providence.

Eugenie Elizabeth, Constance Anderson and Norma were the three Douglas girls. Their father's work took him into stores around Pawtucket. It is easier now to find an address where he worked than a photograph of a window he dressed. A store could change its windows every season. The family kept a clearer picture of the man. He was quiet. He loved to read. They remembered how particular he was about his appearance, right down to his hair.

While the girls were growing up, their mother's family was nearby. In October 1954 her brother, Albert Norman Darcy, died at thirty-eight. Their father, Albert Blake Darcy, the newspaper linotype operator, died in 1957. Janet and Thomas were still in Illinois. Both had become American citizens too, Thomas in 1947 and Janet the following spring.

As in the marriage papers, the family is spread over more than one city. Lizzie appears with the Crombies in the 1940 Chicago census. In Rhode Island one can follow Constance’s Darcy family in directories, draft cards, newspaper notices and the cemetery records in Cranston and Pawtucket. The records fill in different parts of the family table. My mother’s own recollections supply the man at the head of it.

The directory for 1960 names one of the shops where Laurence worked, Carter’s Men Store in Pawtucket. The next directory gives his business in two words, window displays, and prints 644 River Avenue as the address. By the end of his life he was working for himself.

Beside him in the directory is Constance, a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital. She had trained at the Rhode Island School of Practical Nursing. I first came across the two of them in separate entries in a Providence directory, a hairdresser on Westminster and a display manager on Weybosset. Almost a quarter of a century later, the directory lists them together at their home on River Avenue and gives a separate place of work for Constance.

Rhode Island directory entries

1947, Pawtucket, 97 Magill Street. 1950, Providence, 148 General Street. 1956, Providence, 644 River Avenue. The 1960 Providence directory names Carter’s Men Store in Pawtucket. The 1961 edition lists window displays at the River Avenue address.

  2. Providence city directory, 1950, p. 214, 148 General Street. The 1956 and 1959 directory indexes give 644 River Avenue. The author supplied the family’s rental history.

chapters.label: Chapter 30
chapters.title: The Ninth of March
chapters.html:
On Thursday, March 9, 1961, Laurence Brown Douglas died at St. Joseph’s Hospital in Providence. He was fifty-three. My mother remembered how little warning the family had. They understood the illness to be lung cancer. The newspaper described it as a brief illness. I have her account and the newspaper, and each tells the part its author knew.

At the time of his death, Laurence and Constance were renting the house at 644 River Avenue. The city directory listed his window-display business there and his wife, Constance, as a nurse at Roger Williams General Hospital. The woman who had begun her working life dressing hair was nursing by then. The display man who once worked for a national chain was working for himself.

The weather station at T. F. Green Airport in Warwick recorded rain, fog, sleet and snow for March 9. Temperatures ranged from thirty-one to forty-two degrees Fahrenheit. Those are observations from the airport, a few miles south of the city. His Scottish birth register gives an hour. The obituary gives a day for his death, and that is as closely as I can place it.

On Saturday, the Pawtucket Times printed his obituary on page three. It said he had been born in Edinburgh, Scotland. It said he was the son of the late Robert and Elizabeth (Anderson) Douglas. It said he had worked for the Bond Clothing Company, and had his own display business, and that for the past fifteen years he had dressed windows for Pawtucket firms. It named his wife, Constance, their daughters, and his sister, Mrs. Thomas Crombie of Chicago.

The paper also gave the arrangements being made for Monday, March 13. The announced hour was ten in the morning at the Ruth E. Urquhart funeral home, 812 Greenwich Avenue in Warwick. There is a difference between an invitation in a Saturday newspaper and a family memory of who came through the door on Monday. The address and hour are in print. The people in the room are beyond my telling.

The newspaper gave the facts of a working life. The family remembered other things. His friends called him Doug. He was always impeccably dressed, his hair perfectly combed. He was quiet. He loved to read.

The Edinburgh register preserves his mother’s name, Agnes Brown. The Rhode Island obituary preserves the names of the people who raised him, Robert and Elizabeth Douglas. His American citizenship papers bring the two families together in the name he used for himself, Laurence Brown Douglas. That is the name I wanted my mother to have on the cover of her father’s book.

The Pawtucket Times, March 11, 1961, page 3.
Sources and record notes

chapters.label: Epilogue
chapters.title: The Names He Carried
chapters.html:
After Laurence died, Nan went on nursing. The 1963 Warwick directory calls her the widow of Lawrence B. Douglas. It gives her occupation as nurse and her home address as 119 Phillips Avenue. By the time her grandchildren knew her, the watch that had come from Scotland was still in the family. That is the part of its travels I can tell from my own life.

Constance’s obituary remembers her practical-nursing training and eight years at Cranston General Hospital. She retired in 1974. In later life she lived on Sixth Street in East Greenwich and belonged to St. Francis de Sales parish. She died on April 12, 1994, at eighty-one. The Catholic cemetery index places her at Saint Ann in Cranston, in section 5, lot 84. That is a place a grandchild can find.

Janet, the older sister who had left Dunfermline before him, survived him too. The Social Security death index gives December 1979 and a last residence in Maywood, Illinois. She was seventy-nine. In 1940 Lizzie, under the name Elizabeth Anderson, had been counted in Janet’s Chicago household. Twenty-one years later the Rhode Island obituary spoke of both Robert and Elizabeth as deceased. Her final address and the date of her death are particulars I still hope to put beside her name.

Agnes Brown had married Thomas McKenzie in Edinburgh. His Army paper keeps the birthdays of their daughters Mary and Jean. My grandfather had two younger sisters through his birth mother and an older sister, Janet, through the family who raised him. I know a great deal about the bond with Janet because the two of them kept turning up in the same places. I do not know whether he and the McKenzie girls ever met.

I set out to give my grandfather a voice. But more than that, I did it for his daughter, my mother, Constance Douglas, who is eighty-five as I write this. She remembered her father too, and when she spoke of him there was always a little more sadness in it than I ever heard from Nan. I wanted to give him back to her, to make his life real and tangible again.

When I began, a single word inside a watch seemed a small thing to go on. Now the same city appears on a birth register signed by Agnes, on a census that calls her child Lizzie’s son, and on the American papers in which he told his own story. We have the names of the people who answered for him as a boy and the names he gave when it was his turn to answer. We have a photograph of him standing beside his sister, each of them with ice cream. That is a family I can introduce to my mother.

The watch is on my desk as I write this. I can open the case as Nan opened it for me. The engraving still reads Edinburgh.
